label: strategy and planning
overview: Strategy and planning scenarios require the advisor to first diagnose where the client sits — in terms of both their planning maturity and their mindset toward planning — before selecting any template. Four of the tools in this domain work as a natural progression: the Growth Curve Reveal repositions the advisor as a strategic partner; the Heald Matrix surfaces the client's relationship with planning and secures buy-in; the Capacity Capability Opportunity framework diagnoses the real macro constraints; and the Client Planning Framework selects the right planning approach based on business maturity. All planning paths must be supported by a Revenue Model to ensure financial alignment.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the client coming to planning fresh — a startup, new to the concept, or newly motivated — or are they an established business owner who needs a structured strategic review?
diagnostic_entry.client_is_new_to_planning: Use the Growth Curve Reveal to create context and reposition the advisor, then the Heald Matrix to secure planning buy-in, then navigate the Startup branch of the Client Planning Framework.
diagnostic_entry.client_is_established_but_stuck: Use the Heald Matrix to surface the coping mechanism blocking planning progress, then CCO to validate real constraints, then the Well Established Business branch of the Client Planning Framework.
diagnostic_entry.client_wants_strategic_direction: Use CCO to diagnose Capacity, Capability, and Opportunity constraints first — this determines whether the strategic ambition is grounded in reality — then select the appropriate planning template from the Planning Outcomes Review.
diagnostic_entry.revenue_model_always_required: Regardless of which branch is taken, all planning engagements must be supported by a Revenue Model. Financial alignment is not optional — it is the structural backbone of any credible plan.

materials.name: Revealing the Growth Curve
materials.summary: A guided story that walks a client through the nine stages of business growth in the third person, through a persona, so the concept is understood before it is applied to them. Third person creates the dissociation that stops a client judging the idea before they have heard all of it, and gives permission for the humour that makes it stick. Its purpose is alignment and repositioning you as a strategic advisor — not selling.
materials.who_when: Any client not yet engaged with advisory services — particularly inside the EOY meeting or a first advisory conversation, where the relationship needs to move from transactional to strategic.
steps: Position the curve globally first: "This is the Growth Curve — a framework that explains the 9 stages of business growth, from the time a business owner first develops their idea right up until the day they sell it and walk off with a bag of money. We use it with our clients because it highlights the types of issues business owners can expect to encounter BEFORE they have to cope, so they're better prepared and more successful."

Develop your persona before the session: the owner's name, the business name, their age, why they started, and a quirky point of difference — chocolate with rust in it from the washing-machine mixer, or steak and rhubarb pies.

Write the title and draw the framework live, even if your handwriting is bad. Writing it out slows the audience's brain down, draws them into the delivery and creates the focused attention the reveal depends on.
Give yourself plenty of room on the page, and plan ahead to leave gaps for the milestones — break even, lifestyle — so the curve doesn't end up drawn too close to the bottom.
Chunk the phases in blocks of three: write all three down first and only speak to them once they are written. Writing one, explaining it, then writing the next is how you lose your place.
Deliver the whole concept in third person through the persona. If the client is sceptical or resistant, gain agreement that the concept is valid in the persona's case before applying it to theirs.
Then create client relevance: "So where do you think you sit on the curve? What makes you say that? Where do you want to be on the curve, and by when?"

Close without selling: "Now that we're both clear on where you're trying to get to on the curve, would you be open to me offering you ideas or highlighting problem areas — as and when I think they could help you?"

Do not unload strategic observations at this point — there are four possible service solutions to their cash volatility still to come later in the meeting, and a load of observations now will only confuse them.
Diarise a follow-up within 14 days. The four processing styles — Activist, Pragmatist, Reflector, Theorist — mean the client needs a little time to absorb both the concept and your new position.
Practise the delivery at least ten times before the first client: on your partner, your children, the neighbour, or the dog.

materials.name: The Heald Matrix
materials.summary: A two-axis matrix — Innovation and Creativity against Methodology and Process — that shows an owner why they avoid planning, through four positions: Turtle, Shotgun, Lab-Rat and Pioneer. It works because you cannot tell an owner their coping mechanism is not serving them; it is better that they see it themselves and decide to change. Once they have felt how easily they can let it go and gain clarity of action, a planning session stops being something you have to sell.
materials.who_when: Clients resistant to planning, claiming to be too busy, or with no idea where to start. Works in a formal meeting agenda or drawn on a napkin over coffee, which is what shifts a highly formal relationship into a collaborative one.
steps: Listen for the cue — the client admits they don't know the answer to your questions, or says they are too busy for planning.
Ask "Have you heard of the Heald Matrix?" and when they say no, say "Let me show you" and write the title on the page. Writing it buys you time, focuses the client, and creates intrigue.
Draw and label the axes — Innovation/Creativity and Methodology/Process — with high-low or +/- markers so the contrast is visible.

Reveal one quadrant at a time, discussing each before moving on: Turtle (the same old thing the same old way — "if it ain't broke, don't fix it", forgetting that time and tide waits for no man); Shotgun (shoot and hope — creative but lacking data, hope hiding the fear); Lab-Rat (stuck in the grip of fear and judgement, second-guessing, forgetting that trial and error is legitimate testing); Pioneer (fresh ideas balanced with sound process, gratitude for current means combined with excitement for what's new).

Read the behaviour behind it against the three coping styles: Assertion looks like focused and driven, until it drops through the health levels and reads as stubborn and ignorant; Withdrawal looks like considered and prudent, until it reads as lazy and aimless; the third is Dutiful.
Never show the completed matrix all at once — it causes map shock, and the client jumps into assessing all four quadrants instead of buying into the story as you build it.
Ask "Where do you think you sit on the matrix?", then place your pen on the axis of the box they chose and slide it slowly, asking them to say when, so they localise the exact spot.

Ask "WHAT makes you say that?" — never WHY. WHY is inflammatory: it challenges their thinking and sends them looking for an internal defence. WHAT sends them looking for something material and external, which is far less threatening.

Write the word "Evidence" on the board and genuinely look to affirm their position. If they have been hard on themselves, say so and give reasons they may sit elsewhere — the template challenges them internally, so you don't need to be confrontational.

Ask where they would like to be on the matrix in future, then: "IF you took one small baby step towards that, WHAT might that step look like?" IF reduces self-judgement, and one baby step keeps the answer creative rather than defensive.
Validate the baby step they name, however small — looking at the financials once a fortnight counts.

Close with the permission question — "there's a quick example of how we can use cognitive frameworks to improve your creativity and develop ideas to give you a business advantage; would you be open to exploring how we could work a little closer with you going forward?" — and offer an accessible next step, a fortnightly call or a 45-minute session, not a three-day planning summit.
Send the follow-up email summarising what you discussed, attach your branded version of the matrix, and confirm who will call to book the next meeting.

materials.name: Capacity, Capability, Opportunity
materials.summary: A macro-level framework for identifying the legitimate constraints restricting a client's ability to grow, across three pillars: how much the model can produce, whether the client is equipped to compete, and whether the market wants what they sell. Calling them legitimate constraints gives the issues validity and removes the guilt attached to them, which is what lets an owner let go of a limiting belief. It also protects the advisor from picking up every problem-child client and suffering fee creep.
materials.who_when: Used before recommending any strategic direction, and to judge whether a constraint is temporary and better dealt with later. Can be run visibly on the agenda, verbally anchored, or kept as the advisor's own mental checklist where a structured review would feel inappropriate.
steps: Decide how to run it: as your own mental checklist, verbally anchored on the principle points, or written openly on the meeting agenda.
If the client's business model is confusing, bring it back to your own business, look for the similarities, and work out the key variables to explore from there.
Capacity — establish transactional volume: how many widgets or jobs the business model can cope with. Compare the Probable Perfect World output against Current World performance.
Work the capacity model with them and run multiple what-if scenarios; the reveal is what produces the client's own a-ha moment, and the digital models make it far easier.

Say it plainly: "I'm not saying it will be easy to grow your business profits by the figures shown in the model — I'm just saying the figures say it's possible. It's up to us to develop new ideas, test and measure the outcomes and make change where necessary to make the profit a REALITY." Belief is what any significant change of habit rests on.

Capability — assess skill sets and resource: can they deliver premium or volume to their market, handle the larger or more technical jobs, and do they have the tools, equipment and financial resource to play with the big boys?

Where the client is over-optimistic and ready to risk everything, talk them down with "not yet" rather than no. Not yet is not an admission they will never compete; it sends them looking for the evidence of what has to change first, and for the timing that would make it work.
Use capability to explore the future as well: the direction of their industry, the impact of technology, shifts in consumer trends — are they ready to face the new challenges?
Opportunity — demand proof of market demand: what qualitative feedback have existing customers actually given about the growth they are planning?
Identify the event trigger, economy stimulus, fashion driver, technology wave or environmental impact that supports the belief that consumers will want it.

Hold the Goldilocks condition throughout — enough discomfort that the client is motivated to strive for better, not so much that they are paralysed and cannot act on your recommendations. "Fall in love with your customers, not your product or service."

materials.name: Client Planning Framework
materials.summary: Decides which planning approach a client actually needs, based on their business maturity rather than applying one template to everyone. It splits at the first question — a startup or an owner new to planning, against a well-established business — and each branch leads to a different depth of engagement. Whatever the branch, the plan is supported by a Revenue Model, which is what keeps it financially aligned.
materials.who_when: Whenever a client says "I need a business plan" — used once planning buy-in is secured and the real constraints have been validated.
steps: When the client says they need a business plan, ask the clarifying question first: is it for a startup or a well-established business?
For a true startup, use the 1-page or 4-page Bizz Case — excellent for a quick review of business issues, though largely without educative content.

For an owner who is not a startup but is new to planning, use Lite Fundamentals Planning (Lite Strategy): a basic introduction to planning that develops ongoing strategic reviews, with a pre-meeting video designed to put a nervous client at ease.
For a well-established business, bypass the basic plans and start immediately with the Planning Outcomes Review.

Use the Planning Outcomes Review to choose the focus: for Business Targets or Strategic Orientation 1 & 2, use Powerful Goal Setting or the Profit Levers & Blue Ocean templates; for an Organisational Review or a Sales & Marketing Review, use Alignment Statements or the Porter's & Pine templates.

Treat Profit Levers & Blue Ocean and Porter's & Pine as what they are — short-form templates extracted from the advanced strategic templates. Use them to explore deeper issues in their own right and to create client demand for structured, sequential review services such as Management Reporting or Governance Services.
Support every path with a Revenue Model, without exception — startup, new to planning, or well established.

materials.name: Planning Outcomes Review
materials.summary: The broad-scope opening assessment that sets what a planning session will actually cover. It lets the owner explore issues and ideas with an open heart and mind, discover what they have been missing, record key learnings and build an actionable plan forward, giving clarity across the four core planning domains — Business Targets, Strategic Orientation, Organisational Review and Sales & Marketing Review. For the advisor it establishes the role explicitly as challenging what the client believes to be true, structuring the scope of the session and managing collaborative thinking.
materials.who_when: Business owners and leadership teams preparing for a formal business planning session who need a broad scope assessment of their revenue goals, business model, team efficiencies and marketing strategy.
steps: Pre-session preparation: define clear "walk-away" expectations before starting the meeting. Gather past planning documents, financial reports and software models, then select which specific frameworks across the 4 planning domains will be included in the session scope.

Set session roles and mindset: establish that the advisor's role is to challenge existing beliefs, while the client's role is to explore ideas openly. Use De Bono's 6 hats / parallel thinking to manage dominant personalities and maintain collaborative problem-solving.
Execute the domain reviews, walking through the selected planning domains sequentially rather than jumping between them.
Business Targets: define revenue, profit, personal income goals, risk tolerance and work hour expectations.
Strategic Orientation: conduct a challenging review of revenue streams, asset application, target markets and scenario modelling.
Organisational Review: analyse communication channels, divisional roles and individual responsibilities to enhance team engagement.
Sales & Marketing Review: assess customer attention, conversion mechanisms, packaging, pricing and loyalty programmes.
Capture and reflect: employ contrast models (Before–Present–Future). Assign a note-taker to stop every 30 minutes and read back significant points and decisions.
Allow time to "retire and reflect" if core business beliefs are challenged — a belief that has just been dismantled needs space before the next domain is opened.

materials.name: Business Targets
materials.summary: Records what the owner actually wants out of the business — personal income goals, leisure and lifestyle expectations — and then computes the business scale dynamics required to deliver them, finishing with tactical profit lever quick wins. Its method value to the advisor is the structure it gives to parallel (collaborative) thinking during goal setting, which is what avoids time-consuming arguments and the false consensus trap.
materials.who_when: Business owners who need to align personal lifestyle desires with quantifiable operational targets and profit driver actions.
steps: Align the collaborative mindset first: introduce parallel thinking using the 4-sided building analogy, so all participants inspect the same operational aspect together rather than arguing from opposing views.
Log owner expectations: complete the Business Owner Expectations table to record desired personal income, leisure time and leave goals, and effective work habits.

Calculate scale dynamics: complete the Business Development Stages table to compute the required business performance and scale dynamics needed to achieve those personal goals — the dark bands calculate automatically.
Formulate operational objectives: establish clear operational goals that define specific tactical objectives.

Analyse the 8 Profit Levers: review the mathematical formulas for Total Revenue (Foot-traffic × Prospects × Customers × Avg Spend × Frequency) and Total Expenses (Sales Margin + Activity Driven Costs + Fixed Overhead Costs).
Identify quick wins: populate Profit Lever tables 1 and 2 with actionable tasks — if short on time, identify at least 1 task per lever.

materials.name: Orientation Part 1
materials.summary: The formal planning process proper: it educates owners on planning terminology, evaluates internal and external business position, and lands on observable, time-bound operational milestones that are grounded in strategic logic rather than enthusiasm. For the advisor it is a 6-step process taking the client from positional assessment, through scenario modelling, to delegated tactical execution using Field Intelligence.
materials.who_when: Business leaders seeking to establish a shared strategic language across their executive team, conduct SWOT/PEST assessments and build structured action plans.
steps: Assess current position: review pre-gathered team insights, customer insights, financial reports and asset performance, then complete the SWOT analysis table.
Develop strategic scenarios: use the P.E.S.T prompts to identify external drivers, and construct a Scenario Matrix from the two greatest impact drivers.
Determine the Strategic Objective and the Strategy: define a singular, desired end result, then agree the underlying ethos or philosophy that will get them there, using 4-Box Strategic Language.

Set operational objectives: filter every proposed operational goal against three mandatory tests — Observable/Measurable, Time-bound, and Direct support of the Strategic Objective. A goal that fails any one of the three is not an operational objective.
Assign tactics and automated reminders: detail the specific tactical actions (Task, Whom, When) and log them into the Automated Action Plan Reminder.

materials.name: Orientation Part 2
materials.summary: Goes after the reason a mature business has stopped moving. It exposes the psychological growth barriers — the Psyche Errors, such as role-identification or optimism bias — and then introduces the timing frameworks (Sigmoid Curve, Technology Points, Deming Volatility, Blue Ocean) that decide when a business decision or a price change should actually be made. For the advisor it supplies diagnostics for why clients stall, pricing matrices across problem-solving levels and delivery mediums, and a way to model system feedback loops.
materials.who_when: Mature business owners facing growth plateaus, succession friction, product obsolescence, or complex pricing and supply-chain choices.
steps: Identify business stage and Psyche Error: locate the current position on the 7 Growth Focus Tactics curve and diagnose the matching Psyche Errors — Role-Identification, Over-Exposure, Optimism Bias, Complacency, Confirmation Bias.

Apply the market and life cycle frameworks: assess market pressure via Porter's 5 Forces, map product decay on the Product Life Cycle, identify critical price points on Technology Points, and locate point X/Y on the Sigmoid Curve to time new product launches.

Structure pricing and delivery tiers: fill out the Price For Problem Solving table (Free / Tell, Fee / Show, Premium Fee / With, Maximum Fee / For) and the Delivery Medium table (Once to Many, One to Many, One to One).

Analyse integration and revenue options: review Vertical Integration (securing margin vs. quality), Horizontal Integration (consumable/perishable offerings), the Boston Model, the Risk Reward Matrix — testing one unknown at a time — and Upstream/Downstream Revenue Streams.

Map systems and volatility: diagram the system feedback loops using Senge's Circles of Causality, and categorise operational variance into Deming's 4 Volatility Causes — Common, Special, Seasonal and Tampering.

materials.name: Profit Levers & Blue Ocean
materials.summary: Gets an owner off a saturated competition front and turns loose brainstorming into structured quick wins. The Blue Ocean half finds where the customer's frustrations sit on the fringes of normal industry practice; the Profit Lever half sorts the resulting ideas so the incremental gains accumulate rather than scatter. For the advisor it is the fastest route from a wall of post-it notes to a TASK, WHOM, WHEN execution sheet.
materials.who_when: Business owners competing in crowded markets who need clear differentiation, or rapid incremental profit improvements.
steps: Review competition fronts: examine the standard industry competition fronts in the "Red Water Zone" — price, quality, location, consistency.

Map Blue Ocean differentiation: brainstorm the key customer frustrations and frictions, tick the fronts currently focused on, and circle the fronts planned for future competition, so purchasing blockages are removed rather than competed against.
Brainstorm operational activities: write potential activities — pricing, packaging, bundling, brand awareness, inventory, sales messaging — onto post-it notes.
Sort against the 8 Profit Levers: place the post-it notes under the corresponding lever, which is what captures accumulative incremental growth rather than one large bet.
Create the action plan: convert the selected lever tasks into a simple TASK, WHOM, WHEN prioritisation table.

materials.name: SWOT / PEST
materials.summary: The baseline position assessment, run as a dual analysis: SWOT for the internal operational factors — personnel, POS reports, efficiency — and PEST for the external macro-environment of political, economic, regulatory and tariff movement. Its value to the advisor is the prompt set, which is what challenges client assumptions and surfaces growth drag or joint venture potential the owner has not thought to mention.
materials.who_when: Business owners conducting a baseline assessment of their current market standing, or preparing for local or international expansion.
steps: Examine internal position (Strengths and Weaknesses): review internal personnel roles, communication lines, POS report accuracy, profit lines, technology usage, and the financial instruments used to reduce risk or 'growth drag'.
Examine the external environment using the PEST prompts: evaluate the Opportunities and Threats triggered by political, economic, interest rate, consumer confidence, and regulatory or tariff changes.
Assess market capabilities: explore joint venture opportunities, cross-selling potential, customer 'ring fencing' strategies, and technological or environmental industry factors.
Log inputs as they arise, straight into the designated 4-quadrant SWOT/PEST table — recording in the moment rather than reconstructing afterwards.

materials.name: Business Dating
materials.summary: Protects an owner from a hasty amalgamation by making the relationship progressive rather than binary. Four stages — One Night Stand, Dating, Engaged, Married — give both parties a language for where they actually are, so commercial alignment and cultural fit are tested before anything is signed. For the advisor it supplies the narrative and the matrix to walk two entities, often family businesses, through a low-risk alliance ahead of a full merger.
materials.who_when: Business owners considering joint ventures, strategic alliances, family business amalgamations, or business acquisitions.
steps: Classify the relationship stage: categorise the potential relationship into one of the 4 stages — One Night Stand (a singular contract or project), Dating (an ongoing working partnership), Engaged (preparing mentally and financially for merger), or Married (a fully merged entity).
Plot security against commitment: map the prospective alliance onto the 2x2 grid charting Attraction/Security against Attraction/Commitment.

Structure a "business date" instead of an immediate acquisition: a 12-month trial period, with purchase valuations set at the outset and a 12-month right of fulfilment allowing a clean withdrawal. Setting the valuation at the start is what stops the trial itself becoming the negotiation.
Test cultural fit: use the dating period to let teams and stakeholders test the working relationship and integrate cultures under low-strain conditions.

materials.name: Pivot
materials.summary: A rapid 5-step process for a business that has to change direction: identify what is actually forcing the change, refine the message, and test a prototype offering at minimal risk rather than committing the business to an untested bet. For the advisor it is a structured pipeline through a forced change, including a high-converting AIDCRA advertisement and strict test parameters agreed before anything is spent.
materials.who_when: Agile business owners needing to pivot their strategy quickly, introduce new products, or overcome market resistance.
steps: Identify the resistance: analyse market pressure using Porter's 5 Forces, Market Diffusion Theory (the 15% tipping point), the Product Life Cycle, Technology Points and the Sigmoid Curve, to answer "What's forcing the change?".
Choose competition fronts: select fronts across the Blue Ocean, Vertical or Horizontal Integration models, and log the initial observations and responses.

Rehearse the message: answer the 6 Critical Marketing Questions — target profile, concerns, constraints, special factors, value added, messaging channels — then build the ad using the AIDCRA framework (Attention, Interest, Desire, Credibility, Risk Removal, Action).

Trial the prototype: define budget and timeline test parameters for product development, market research, competitor analysis, team learning, prototype solution and messaging appeal — set before the trial starts, not judged after it.
Do it and review it: execute the prototype trial within the set parameters and evaluate the performance metrics against them.

materials.name: Porters & Pine
materials.summary: A dual-framework session that does two things at once: reads the competitive pressure on the business, and moves its offering up the economic value chain from commoditised goods towards authentic, high-margin customer experience. The engine of the second half is genuine customer connection — that is what premium pricing and retention actually rest on, rather than presentation.
materials.who_when: Business owners operating in traditional service or commodity markets who are seeking to increase profit margins and build customer loyalty.
steps: Assess the 5 Forces pressure: evaluate Customers, Suppliers, Substitutes, New Entrants and Existing Rivals to determine the expected threats, opportunities and financial returns.
Map the economic value progression: trace the product or service offering along Pine's Progression of Economic Value — Commodity → Goods → Services → Experience → Authenticity.

Align imperatives and sensitivities: pair each economic output with its corresponding business imperative and consumer sensitivity — Commodity/Supply/Availability, Goods/Quality Control/Costs, Services/Improve/Quality, Experience/Render/Authenticity.
Establish customer connection: implement the mechanisms that bring owner and customer onto the same emotional level, through sincere efforts to 'connect' rather than staged ones.
Document the strategy: fill out the Progression of Economic Development table to record the observations and the strategic responses.

advisor_guidance.sequence_matters: These four tools work as a natural progression — Growth Curve to open and reposition, Heald Matrix to secure planning buy-in, CCO to validate real constraints, Client Planning Framework to select the right template. Jumping straight to a planning template without the earlier steps is the most common reason planning engagements feel forced or are resisted.
advisor_guidance.do_not_sell_after_the_reveal: The Growth Curve and Heald Matrix both close with low-pressure permission questions — not sales pitches. The strategic repositioning is undone the moment an advisor immediately lists advisory services. Secure permission, book a next step, follow up within 14 days.
advisor_guidance.not_yet_over_no: When a client's ambitions exceed their current capability, NOT YET is far more productive than a blunt correction. It redirects without crushing and immediately prompts the client to think about what they need to change — turning a potential deflation into a development conversation.
advisor_guidance.revenue_model_is_non_negotiable: Every planning path — startup, new to planning, or well established — requires a Revenue Model. A plan without financial alignment is a wish list. The Revenue Model is what converts strategic intention into something the client can actually test, measure, and hold themselves accountable to.
